The same supper, received as a gift from a Father's hand.

3.title: A Time for Everything, and Eternity in the Heart

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — A Time for Every Matter Under Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven (v. 1). Fourteen pairs follow, from birth and death, planting and uprooting (v. 2), through killing and healing, weeping and laughing, mourning and dancing (vv. 3-4), gathering and casting away, seeking and losing, tearing and sewing, silence and speech (vv. 5-7), to a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Every moment of a human life has its appointed time, and the one who appoints the times is God.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:

This is one of the best-known passages in the Bible, read at funerals, set to music and quoted by people who have never opened Ecclesiastes. It is usually heard as gentle poetry about the rhythms of life. In the Preacher's mouth it is something stronger.

Chapter 1 showed the world going round and round. Chapter 3 shows that the round is not random. For everything there is a season. Every event in a human life has its appointed moment, and the rest of the chapter makes clear who appointed it: He has made everything beautiful in its time (v. 11). The seasons of life are not merely what happens. They are what God has set.

That can feel like a cage or like a comfort, depending on what you believe about the one who sets the times. The psalmist, surrounded by enemies, found it a comfort: My times are in your hand (Ps 31:15).

verseByVerse.quote: a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted; a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
verseByVerse.commentary:
a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted;

The list begins at the edges of life. No one chose the time of his birth, and no one chooses the time of his death. Everything else falls between those two appointments. Then the farmer's year: planting and uprooting. A farmer who plants in the wrong season loses the crop, however hard he works.

The poem is built of fourteen pairs of opposites, twenty-eight times in all. By setting opposites side by side, it covers the whole of life, from one end to the other, the way "day and night" means all the time.

a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;

A time to kill is not a licence for private violence. Scripture gives the sword to rightful authority, for justice: Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed (Gen 9:6), and the ruler does not bear the sword in vain (Rom 13:4). There is a time when justice or defence requires it, and a time when healing is called for.

Break down and build up belong together too. A house that is rotten must sometimes be torn down before a sound one can be built. That is true of habits, of churches, and of hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
verseByVerse.commentary:
a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;

Emotions have their seasons. The Christian life is not a permanent smile. There are funerals, and it is right to weep at them. Jesus wept at the grave of his friend. There are weddings, and it is right to dance. Wisdom is knowing which room you are in. Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). Telling a grieving friend to cheer up is not faith. It is getting the time wrong.

a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;

The meaning of casting away and gathering stones is not certain. It may picture a farmer clearing stones from a field and a builder collecting them for a wall. Whatever the exact picture, it sits beside embracing and refraining, and the pairing suggests coming close and holding back. There is a time for closeness and a time for distance, a time to hold someone near and a time to let them go.

verseByVerse.quote: a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away; a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;

There is a time to go looking for what is lost, and a time to accept that it is gone. There is a time to hold on to possessions, and a time to clear them out. Anyone who has emptied a parent's house after a death knows both halves of this verse in a single afternoon.

a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;

Tearing a garment was the sign of grief in Israel, and sewing is the ordinary work of mending. There is a time for each. And there is a time for silence and a time to speak. Job's friends did best in the first seven days, when they said nothing. The wisest words are often the ones not spoken yet, and there are also moments when silence is cowardice.

a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.

The poem ends with the largest opposites. A time to hate startles us, but Scripture does not ask us to feel nothing about evil. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good (Rom 12:9). The psalmist could say, Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD? (Ps 139:21). A person who cannot hate cruelty does not truly love its victims.

And the list ends with peace. Every time in the poem has its place, but the last word is the one toward which God is bringing history. The time the whole Bible looks toward is the one Paul calls the fullness of time, when God sent forth his Son (Gal 4:4). Jesus lived by his Father's times: My hour has not yet come (John 2:4), and at the end, Father, the hour has come (John 17:1). At the right time Christ died for the ungodly (Rom 5:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What gain has the worker from his toil? (v. 9). God has given the business of life (v. 10). He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet man cannot find out the whole of God's work (v. 11). So there is nothing better than to be joyful, to do good, and to receive food and work as God's gift to man (vv. 12-13). What God does endures forever, so that people fear before him (v. 14), and God seeks what has been driven away (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: We are made for eternity and cannot see it whole; God's gifts are to be received now, and God himself feared.

verseByVerse.quote: What gain has the worker from his toil? I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What gain has the worker from his toil?

After the poem, the question of 1:3 again. If God has set every time, what can our work add? We cannot change the seasons. We plant when it is time to plant and die when it is time to die. So where is the gain?

I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.

In 1:13 the Preacher called this business unhappy. Here he simply says God has given it. He is looking at the same fact from a slightly higher place. The work of life is not a meaningless accident. It is an assignment, and the one who assigned it knows why.

verseByVerse.quote: He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has made everything beautiful in its time.

This is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament. Everything, even the times of weeping, losing and dying, is beautiful in its time. Not beautiful in isolation. A funeral is not beautiful as a funeral. But set in its time, in the whole design, it has a place that makes the design good.

Think of a tapestry seen from behind: knots, loose threads, colours that make no sense. Turn it over and the picture appears. Joseph lived more than twenty years on the wrong side of the tapestry, and at the end he could say to his brothers, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen 50:20). We know that for those who love God all things work together for good (Rom 8:28).

Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end.

Here is the reason human beings cannot be content with the treadmill of chapter 1. God has put eternity into man's heart. Animals do not ask what their life means. People do. We long for things to last, for love not to end, for justice to be done, for the dead not to be lost. That longing is not a fantasy; it was put there by God. It is why nothing under the sun satisfies.

But the same verse puts a limit on it: we cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end. We have eternity in the heart and a few decades in the hand. We can sense the shape of the whole and cannot see it. Only God is declaring the end from the beginning (Isa 46:10). So we live, as Paul says, seeing in a mirror dimly, but then face to face (1 Cor 13:12).

The longing for eternity is finally a longing for God, and it is met in Christ, who said, I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25).

verseByVerse.quote: I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live; also that everyone should eat and drink and take pleasure in all his toil—this is God's gift to man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live;

If we cannot see the whole, what should we do? The Preacher's answer is the second of his "nothing better" passages (2:24). Be joyful, and do good. Two simple things, and they belong together. Joy without doing good is selfish; doing good without joy is grim. As long as they live: not someday, when the whole picture makes sense, but now.

also that everyone should eat and drink and take pleasure in all his toil—this is God's gift to man.

The ordinary things: meals, drink, daily work. The Preacher calls them God's gift to man. A person who cannot see how the whole of his life fits together can still sit at his table tonight and thank God for the bread. That is not a small thing. It is the life of faith in its daily form. For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Tim 4:4).

verseByVerse.quote: I perceived that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before him. That which is, already has been; that which is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I perceived that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before him.

Human work evaporates, as chapters 1 and 2 showed. God's work stands. Whatever God does endures forever. No one can improve on it or undo it. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa 40:8).

And God's purpose in making it so is stated: so that people fear before him. This is the first mention of the fear of God in the book, and it is where the book will end (12:13). When a person realises that his own work is breath and God's work is permanent, the right response is reverent awe. The fear of God is not terror before a tyrant. It is taking God seriously as God.

That which is, already has been; that which is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away.

The first half echoes 1:9. The second half is new and full of hope. The ESV notes that what has been driven away is in Hebrew "what has been pursued". The past seems gone, chased away by time. But God goes after it. Nothing is lost to him. He calls the past back to account, and he calls the lost back home.

That is the heart of God throughout Scripture: I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed (Ezek 34:16). And it is the mission of his Son: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). If you feel driven away, you are exactly the kind of person God seeks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–22 — Injustice, Judgment and the Dust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wickedness sits even in the place of justice (v. 16), but God will judge the righteous and the wicked (v. 17). God tests people to show them they are like beasts: All are from the dust, and to dust all return (vv. 18-20). Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward? (v. 21). So a man should rejoice in his work, for no one can show him what comes after (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Under the sun, man and beast die alike; above the sun, God will judge, and the spirit returns to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, even there was wickedness. I said in my heart, God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moreover, I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, even there was wickedness.

The Preacher turns from the beauty of God's times to the ugliness of human injustice. And he finds wickedness in the worst place, the place of justice: the courtroom. When the judge is corrupt, where can the wronged go? Every generation sees it: the bribed official, the rigged trial, the powerful who are never held to account.

I said in my heart, God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work.

And here he rises above the sun. God will judge. The poem of verses 1-8 named no time for judgment, and here it is: there is a time for every matter and for every work, and that includes the verdict. The corrupt judge has his day in court coming. Every injustice will be set right.

The New Testament names the day and the judge: God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). For the oppressed, that is the best news there is. For all of us, it is a reason to flee to the judge while he is still offering mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart with regard to the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts. For what happens to the children of man and what happens to the beasts is the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity. All go to one place. All are from the dust, and to dust all return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I said in my heart with regard to the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts.

The same injustice has a second lesson. When people behave like animals, devouring one another in the courts, God lets them see what they are without him. Pride says, we are the masters of the world. Death answers, you are creatures. Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish (Ps 49:20).

For what happens to the children of man and what happens to the beasts is the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity.

From under the sun, this is simply true. Watch a man die and a dog die, and the body does the same thing. Both stop breathing. When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust (Ps 104:29).

All go to one place. All are from the dust, and to dust all return.

These are God's words to Adam: for you are dust, and to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19). The one place is the grave. No one skips it. The Preacher wants his hearers to feel it, because only a person who knows he is dust will look to God for life.

verseByVerse.quote: Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?

From under the sun, no one can prove what happens after death. The Preacher does not deny that the human spirit goes upward; he says that observation cannot settle it. Nobody has come back to report.

But the book does not stop at the question. The same Preacher will say at the end that the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it (12:7). What sight cannot establish, God has revealed.

And the New Testament goes further, because someone has come back. Christ Jesus abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (2 Tim 1:10). Paul knew where the believer's spirit goes: we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Cor 5:8). The dying thief heard it from Christ himself: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). The question "Who knows?" has an answer, and his name is Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?

The chapter ends where the "nothing better" passages always land. Since you cannot see the future, and cannot control what comes after you, rejoice in his work. It is your lot, your portion, the share God has assigned.

This is not resignation. It is freedom. The person who must see how everything turns out before he can be at peace will never be at peace. The person who does today's work gladly, as his portion from God, and leaves the future with God, can rest. Paul put it this way: Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward (Col 3:23-24).

What is the work in front of you tomorrow morning? Do it as your lot from God, and leave the rest to him.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:<sup>2</sup>a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted;<sup>3</sup>a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;<sup>4</sup>a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;<sup>5</sup>a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;<sup>6</sup>a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;<sup>7</sup>a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;<sup>8</sup>a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.<sup>9</sup>What gain has the worker from his toil?<sup>10</sup>I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.<sup>11</sup>He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end.<sup>12</sup>I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live;<sup>13</sup>also that everyone should eat and drink and take pleasure in all his toil—this is God's gift to man.<sup>14</sup>I perceived that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before him.<sup>15</sup>That which is, already has been; that which is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away.<sup>16</sup>Moreover, I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, even there was wickedness.<sup>17</sup>I said in my heart, God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work.<sup>18</sup>I said in my heart with regard to the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts.<sup>19</sup>For what happens to the children of man and what happens to the beasts is the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity.<sup>20</sup>All go to one place. All are from the dust, and to dust all return.<sup>21</sup>Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?<sup>22</sup>So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?
3.overview:
For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven (v. 1). Fourteen pairs of opposites, from birth and death to war and peace, cover the whole of life and show that every moment has its appointed time (vv. 2-8).

What gain, then, does the worker have (v. 9)? God has made everything beautiful in its time and has put eternity into man's heart, though man cannot find out the whole of God's work (vv. 10-11). So there is nothing better than to rejoice, do good and receive food and work as God's gift (vv. 12-13). God's work endures, so that people fear him, and God seeks what has been driven away (vv. 14-15).

Wickedness sits in the place of justice, but God will judge (vv. 16-17). Man and beast die alike and return to dust, and no one under the sun can see what follows (vv. 18-21). So a man should rejoice in his work, which is his lot (v. 22).
3.theology:
God appoints every time of human life (vv. 1-8; Ps 31:15) and makes everything beautiful in its time (v. 11; Rom 8:28). He has set eternity in the human heart, so that nothing temporal can satisfy, while keeping the whole of his purpose beyond our sight (v. 11; Isa 46:10; 1 Cor 13:12).

God's work endures and is meant to produce reverent fear (v. 14). God seeks what has been driven away (v. 15; Luke 19:10). He will judge the righteous and the wicked (v. 17), and has fixed the day by the risen Christ (Acts 17:31).

Under the sun, man dies like the beasts (vv. 18-20; Gen 3:19). The question of v. 21 is answered in 12:7 and fully in the gospel, which has brought life and immortality to light (2 Tim 1:10).
3.examples:
The farmer who plants in the wrong season.

Telling a grieving friend to cheer up.

Emptying a parent's house in a single afternoon.

A tapestry seen from behind.

The bribed judge who has his own day in court coming.

Tomorrow morning's work, done as your lot from God.

4.title: Tears, Envy and the Threefold Cord

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Tears with No One to Comfort
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher sees the oppressions done under the sun: the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them! Power is on the side of the oppressors (v. 1). He calls the dead more fortunate than the living (v. 2), and the one never born better than both, because he has not seen the evil deeds that are done under the sun (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: Under the sun, the oppressed have no comforter; the God of all comfort is the answer the chapter longs for.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. And behold, the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them! On the side of their oppressors there was power, and there was no one to comfort them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. And behold, the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them!

In chapter 3 the Preacher saw wickedness in the courtroom and held on to the truth that God will judge. But judgment is future, and the tears are now. So he looks again, and this time he sees the faces. Behold, the tears of the oppressed. The worker cheated of wages, the widow whose land was taken, the child sold, the prisoner beaten. And the saddest words: they had no one to comfort them.

On the side of their oppressors there was power, and there was no one to comfort them.

He says it twice. That repetition is a cry. The oppressors have power; the oppressed have no one. Lamentations has the same grief: my eyes flow with tears; for a comforter is far from me (Lam 1:16).

The Bible does not look away from this, and Christians must not either. Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated (Heb 13:3). And the Bible answers the double cry with a double name: the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction (2 Cor 1:3-4). The one who was himself oppressed and stood silent before his accusers promised his followers another Helper, to be with you forever (John 14:16). No believer is left with no one to comfort him, and no believer should leave the oppressed with no one either.

verseByVerse.quote: And I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive. But better than both is he who has not yet been and has not seen the evil deeds that are done under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive. But better than both is he who has not yet been and has not seen the evil deeds that are done under the sun.

This is as dark as Scripture gets. Better to be dead than to watch this. Better never to have been born. Job said it: Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire? (Job 3:11). So did Jeremiah: Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow (Jer 20:18).

God put these words in his book, and that is a kindness. People crushed by what they have seen, soldiers, social workers, survivors, need to know that the Bible has been there and said it aloud. The Preacher is not recommending death. He is saying how heavy the weight of evil is when it is seen only from under the sun. If you have felt this, say it to God as honestly as these men did, and then keep reading. The book does not stop here, and neither does God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — Envy, Idleness and the Lonely Miser
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Much toil is driven by a man's envy of his neighbor (v. 4). The fool who does nothing destroys himself (v. 5), yet Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind (v. 6). And there is the man alone, with no son or brother, working endlessly and never asking, For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure? (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Work driven by envy or greed empties the worker; a quiet handful is richer than two restless fists.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.

From oppression by others to a sickness within. Why do people work so hard? The Preacher's uncomfortable answer: much of it is envy. The bigger house next door, the colleague's promotion, the friend's holiday photos. We call it ambition, drive, keeping up. He calls it envy, and he calls it breath.

Not every act of work is envious, and he says so elsewhere. But ask yourself honestly how much of your effort would continue if no one else could see the result. A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot (Prov 14:30). The gospel frees a person to work for others rather than against them: Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others (Phil 2:4).

verseByVerse.quote: The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh. Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh.

The opposite of envious overwork is not the answer either. The fool who stops working altogether consumes himself. He does not starve because others stole from him; he starves by doing nothing. A little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber (Prov 6:10-11).

Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind.

Here is the wise middle. Picture three pairs of hands. The fool's are folded: nothing. The envious worker's are both full, clutching, and his heart has no rest. The wise person has one hand full and is at peace. A handful is enough when it comes with quietness.

Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it (Prov 15:16). Would you trade some of your income for more peace? Many people who say no are already paying for their income with their peace. Jesus offers what the overfilled hands cannot hold: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: Again, I saw vanity under the sun: one person who has no other, either son or brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches, so that he never asks, "For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?" This also is vanity and an unhappy business.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again, I saw vanity under the sun: one person who has no other, either son or brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches,

A new portrait: the man alone. No children, no brothers, no one to share with or leave anything to. And he works without end. His eyes, like the eyes of 1:8, are never satisfied. He does not need more. He simply cannot stop.

so that he never asks, "For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?" This also is vanity and an unhappy business.

The tragedy is not only his loneliness but the question he never asks. For whom am I toiling? He is depriving himself of every pleasure in order to pile up money that will go to no one he loves. The rich fool in Jesus' parable heard the same question from God: the things you have prepared, whose will they be? (Luke 12:20).

Ask it of your own week. For whom are you working? If the honest answer is "no one, really", something has gone wrong that more money will not fix.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — Two Are Better Than One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two are better than one: they share the reward (v. 9), lift each other when one falls (v. 10), keep each other warm (v. 11), and stand together against an attacker, for a threefold cord is not quickly broken (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: God did not make people to live alone, and the answer to the lonely miser is companionship.

verseByVerse.quote: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil.

Against the lonely miser, the Preacher sets companionship. Two are better than one. It is the first thing in all creation that God called not good: It is not good that the man should be alone (Gen 2:18). Work shared has a better reward, because it is shared.

For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!

Everyone falls: into sin, into sickness, into grief, into a ditch on a dark road. The question is not whether you will fall, but whether anyone will be there when you do. Woe to him who is alone. The man who has kept everyone at a distance finds, when he falls, that there is no one close enough to reach him.

This is one reason God puts believers in churches. Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ (Gal 6:2). Who would lift you up if you fell tomorrow? And whom are you close enough to lift?

verseByVerse.quote: Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone? And though a man might prevail against one who is alone, two will withstand him—a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone?

A traveller's picture: a cold night on the road, and two people sharing warmth. It applies to marriage, but not only to marriage. Friendship, fellowship and family all keep a person warm in a cold world.

And though a man might prevail against one who is alone, two will withstand him—a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

A robber can overpower one traveller. Two stand him off. And if two are strong, three are stronger still: a threefold cord is not quickly broken. Twist three strands together and the rope holds what none of them could hold alone.

The verse is often read at weddings, with Christ as the third strand between husband and wife. That is not what the Preacher first meant; he was talking about companions in general. But it is a true application. A marriage, or a friendship, bound together with Christ holds in the storm. Let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together (Heb 10:24-25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — The Wise Youth and the Fickle Crowd
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Better was a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knew how to take advice (v. 13). The youth rises from prison to the throne (v. 14), and all the people follow him (vv. 15-16). Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Popularity is breath. The crowd that crowns a king today will forget him tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Better was a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knew how to take advice. For he went from prison to the throne, though in his own kingdom he had been born poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better was a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knew how to take advice.

Now a short story. An old king, once perhaps wise, has become the kind of man who cannot be told anything. Age and power do not guarantee wisdom; they often destroy teachability. A poor young man with sense is better off than the king who has stopped listening.

For he went from prison to the throne, though in his own kingdom he had been born poor.

The youth rises from nothing, from prison, to the crown. The Bible has such stories: Joseph was brought out of the pit and stood before Pharaoh the same day (Gen 41:14), and David was a shepherd boy before he was king. It is a great reversal, and everyone loves it.

verseByVerse.quote: I saw all the living who move about under the sun, along with that youth who was to stand in the king's place. There was no end of all the people, all of whom he led. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I saw all the living who move about under the sun, along with that youth who was to stand in the king's place.

Everyone flocks to the new man. The ESV notes that that youth is in Hebrew "the second": the one who comes next, the successor. The whole population moves to his side.

There was no end of all the people, all of whom he led. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind.

And then the sting. Those who come later will not rejoice in him. The next generation will not remember his rise from prison. They will want their own new face. The crowd that crowned him will move on.

Popularity is breath. Every leader, pastor, celebrity and politician learns it. Jerusalem's crowds shouted Hosanna to Jesus as he rode in, and within the week a crowd was shouting for his death. He never entrusted himself to the crowd's applause, and the one King worth following is the one whose kingdom does not depend on the crowd's favour. The poor, wise youth who rose from the grave to the throne is not replaced by a successor. His reign has no end.

On the side of their oppressors there was power, and there was no one to comfort them.<sup>2</sup>And I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive.<sup>3</sup>But better than both is he who has not yet been and has not seen the evil deeds that are done under the sun.<sup>4</sup>Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind.
4.overview:
The Preacher sees the tears of the oppressed, with power on the side of the oppressors and no one to comfort them (v. 1). He calls the dead more fortunate than the living, and the unborn better still (vv. 2-3).

He sees that much toil comes from envy (v. 4). The fool who folds his hands destroys himself, yet a handful of quietness is better than two hands full of toil (vv. 5-6). A man with no son or brother works without end and never asks for whom he toils (vv. 7-8).

Two are better than one: companions lift, warm and defend one another, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken (vv. 9-12). A poor, wise youth who rises from prison to the throne is better than an old king who will not take advice, but even he is forgotten by those who come later (vv. 13-16).
4.theology:
Scripture looks honestly at oppression and at the despair it produces (vv. 1-3; Job 3:11; Jer 20:18). The answer to the cry for a comforter is the God of all comfort (2 Cor 1:3-4) and the Helper Christ promised (John 14:16), and his people are to comfort the oppressed (Heb 13:3).

Envy corrupts work, and idleness destroys the idle; contentment with quietness is better (vv. 4-6; Prov 15:16). God made people for companionship (vv. 9-12; Gen 2:18) and gives the church to bear one another's burdens (Gal 6:2). Human popularity is fleeting (vv. 13-16); only Christ's reign has no end.
4.examples:
Working harder because of the neighbour's bigger house.

Three pairs of hands: folded, clutching, and one handful at rest.

The man with no heirs who cannot stop working.

Falling on a dark road with no one near enough to help.

Hosanna on Sunday and "Crucify" on Friday.

5.title: Guard Your Steps: Worship, Vows and the Love of Money

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Guard Your Steps in the House of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. Listening is better than the sacrifice of fools (v. 1). God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few (vv. 2-3). Pay what you vow, and do not call it a mistake afterward (vv. 4-6). Many words are vanity, but God is the one you must fear (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: True worship begins with listening to God, and reverence shows itself in few, honest words.

verseByVerse.quote: Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Guard your steps when you go to the house of God.

After four chapters of observing life under the sun, the Preacher suddenly speaks in commands, and the first place he sends us is the house of God. If life is breath and the world cannot satisfy, how should a person approach the God who stands above it all? Carefully. Guard your steps. Watch how you walk in.

To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil.

The fool comes to worship to do something: bring his offering, say his piece, tick the box. The wise person comes to listen. Samuel told Saul the same thing: to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams (1 Sam 15:22). And the fool does not even know it. They do not know that they are doing evil. He thinks religious activity pleases God regardless of his heart. This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me (Matt 15:8).

What do you come to church to do? The verse says the first thing is to hear. Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak (Jas 1:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Be not rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few. For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with many words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few.

Here is the reason for reverence: God is in heaven and you are on earth. The distance between Creator and creature is infinite. Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases (Ps 115:3). So the fitting response is not a flood of words, but few words, carefully meant.

Jesus taught the same: when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words (Matt 6:7). And then he taught his disciples a prayer that begins, "Our Father in heaven". Both halves matter. He is in heaven, so we come with awe. He is our Father, so we come without fear. In Christ we may with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb 4:16), and still offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire (Heb 12:28-29). Confidence without reverence becomes chatter. Reverence without confidence becomes dread.

For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with many words.

A busy mind produces restless dreams, and a foolish person produces a stream of talk. Many words are a mark of the fool, in prayer as much as anywhere.

verseByVerse.quote: When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow. It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay. Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow. It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay.

A vow was a voluntary promise to God, often made in a moment of need: if you rescue me, I will give you this. The law said the same as the Preacher: If you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay fulfilling it and if you refrain from vowing, you will not be guilty of sin (Deut 23:21-22). No one has to make a vow. But a promise to God is not a mood. It is a debt.

Think of the promises made in hospital waiting rooms and on sinking boats, and forgotten when the danger passed. It is a snare to say rashly, "It is holy," and to reflect only after making vows (Prov 20:25). Jephthah made a rash vow and lived to say, I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow (Judg 11:35). Ananias and Sapphira pretended to give everything and kept part back, and Peter said, You have not lied to man but to God (Acts 5:4).

Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?

The ESV notes that your mouth is in Hebrew "your flesh", and that messenger may be rendered "angel". The picture is of a person going back on his promise before God's representative and excusing it as an honest mistake. God is not fooled.

Christians make vows too: at baptism, at marriage, at membership, at ordination. Jesus' rule covers all our words: Let what you say be simply 'Yes' or 'No' (Matt 5:37). Is there a promise you made to God that you have quietly reclassified as a mistake?

verseByVerse.quote: For when dreams increase and words grow many, there is vanity; but God is the one you must fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when dreams increase and words grow many, there is vanity; but God is the one you must fear.

The section ends with its conclusion. Dreams and many words are breath, hebel again, as the ESV's note says. The note also offers another rendering, "For when dreams and vanities increase, words also grow many", but on either reading the contrast is the same. Religious talk, spiritual feelings and elaborate promises can all be vapour.

What is solid? God is the one you must fear. This is the second time the book has named the fear of God (3:14), and it stands here as the centre of true worship. It is not a feeling to work up, but a settled seriousness about who God is. A person who fears God will say less to him and mean more of it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oppression in a province should not amaze anyone, for officials watch officials, all the way up (vv. 8-9). He who loves money will not be satisfied with money (v. 10). More goods bring more eaters (v. 11), and Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, while the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Money promises satisfaction and security; it delivers neither.

verseByVerse.quote: If you see in a province the oppression of the poor and the violation of justice and righteousness, do not be amazed at the matter, for the high official is watched by a higher, and there are yet higher ones over them. But this is gain for a land in every way: a king committed to cultivated fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you see in a province the oppression of the poor and the violation of justice and righteousness, do not be amazed at the matter, for the high official is watched by a higher, and there are yet higher ones over them.

From the house of God to the halls of government. The Preacher is a realist. When you see the poor oppressed and justice denied in the provinces, do not be amazed. Layers of officials watch one another, each protecting his own position and taking his cut. Bureaucracy can hide injustice as easily as it prevents it.

But read the ladder to the top. Above the highest official there is one higher still. God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment (Ps 82:1). No official is finally unaccountable. There is no authority except from God (Rom 13:1), and every authority will answer to him.

But this is gain for a land in every way: a king committed to cultivated fields.

The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew in this verse is uncertain, so it should be held with a light hand. As the ESV renders it, the Preacher sets against the self-serving officials a king whose concern is the productive land, the fields that feed the people. Government that serves the ordinary work of ordinary people is a gain to everyone.

verseByVerse.quote: He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with his income; this also is vanity. When goods increase, they increase who eat them, and what advantage has their owner but to see them with his eyes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with his income; this also is vanity.

Few sentences about money have been proved true more often. He who loves money will not be satisfied with money. Ask any lottery winner, or anyone who has earned more this year than last. Money promises that the next level will be enough, and when you reach it, it has moved.

Money is not the problem. The love of it is. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Tim 6:10). The cure is not poverty but contentment rooted in God's presence: Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, "I will never leave you nor forsake you" (Heb 13:5).

When goods increase, they increase who eat them, and what advantage has their owner but to see them with his eyes?

More income brings more mouths: staff, advisers, tax, maintenance, relatives, and a bigger house to heat. The owner's only advantage is looking at what he has. The larger the estate, the more of it is consumed by others. One's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions (Luke 12:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep.

A labourer who has worked hard all day sleeps well, whether his supper was large or small. The rich man lies awake, too full to rest, and too anxious about what he has. His stomach and his mind are both overloaded.

Sleep is one thing money cannot buy. The psalmist found the secret of it in God: You have put more joy in my heart than they have when their grain and wine abound. In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Ps 4:7-8). Where does your mind go when you cannot sleep? It often shows where your treasure is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Riches Lost, and Naked We Go
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Riches hoarded to the owner's hurt are lost in a bad venture, and he has nothing to leave his son (vv. 13-14). As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came (v. 15). He toiled for the wind, and ate all his days in darkness and vexation (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Everyone leaves the world with empty hands; the only question is what he lived for.

verseByVerse.quote: There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches were kept by their owner to his hurt, and those riches were lost in a bad venture. And he is father of a son, but he has nothing in his hand. As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came, and shall take nothing for his toil that he may carry away in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches were kept by their owner to his hurt, and those riches were lost in a bad venture. And he is father of a son, but he has nothing in his hand.

A story everyone has seen. A man hoards his wealth, and the hoarding hurts him. Then it is gone in one bad investment, a failed business, a crash. And he has a son, and nothing to give him. All the years of saving and denying produced an empty hand.

As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came, and shall take nothing for his toil that he may carry away in his hand.

And even if the venture had succeeded, the end would be the same. We arrive naked, and we leave naked. Job said it as he lost everything: Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return (Job 1:21). Paul said it to Timothy: we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world (1 Tim 6:7). There are no pockets in a shroud.

But Jesus showed a way to send treasure ahead: Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail (Luke 12:33).

verseByVerse.quote: This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain is there to him who toils for the wind? Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain is there to him who toils for the wind?

The question of 1:3 again, and a new picture: toils for the wind. A lifetime of work, and the wages paid in wind. That is what it is to work only for what we can keep.

Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger.

And the hoarder did not even enjoy the journey. He ate in darkness: anxious, resentful, ill, angry. The love of money did not only fail to give him a future. It took his present. Paul says that some who craved money have pierced themselves with many pangs (1 Tim 6:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What is good and fitting is to eat, drink and enjoy one's toil in the few days God gives (v. 18). The power to enjoy wealth and accept one's lot is the gift of God (v. 19), and God keeps such a person occupied with joy in his heart (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The ability to enjoy what we have is itself God's gift, and it frees us from the anxious counting of days.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil with which one toils under the sun the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his lot. Everyone also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil—this is the gift of God. For he will not much remember the days of his life because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil with which one toils under the sun the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his lot.

After the dark portrait, the "nothing better" passage returns (2:24; 3:12-13, 22), and it begins with Behold. Look at this instead. What is good and fitting is simple: eat, drink, enjoy your work, in the few days of life that God has given. The ESV notes that find enjoyment may be rendered "see good". The hoarder ate in darkness; the one who receives life from God sees the good.

Everyone also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil—this is the gift of God.

Notice the three gifts. Wealth is a gift. The power to enjoy it is a second, separate gift, and chapter 6 will show a man who had the first without the second. And the ability to accept his lot, to be content with the portion God has given, is a third. Godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Tim 6:6). The rich are to set their hope on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy, and to be generous and ready to share (1 Tim 6:17-18).

For he will not much remember the days of his life because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.

A lovely ending. The person who receives life as God's gift is not constantly counting his days, brooding on how short life is or how little he has. God keeps him occupied with joy. Like a child absorbed in play who forgets to watch the clock, he is too busy enjoying God's gifts to be consumed by anxiety about losing them. That is the opposite of the hoarder who ate in darkness, and it is God's gift, not a technique.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil.<sup>2</sup>Be not rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few.<sup>3</sup>For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with many words.<sup>4</sup>When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow.<sup>5</sup>It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay.<sup>6</sup>Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?<sup>7</sup>For when dreams increase and words grow many, there is vanity; but God is the one you must fear.<sup>8</sup>If you see in a province the oppression of the poor and the violation of justice and righteousness, do not be amazed at the matter, for the high official is watched by a higher, and there are yet higher ones over them.<sup>9</sup>But this is gain for a land in every way: a king committed to cultivated fields.<sup>10</sup>He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with his income; this also is vanity.<sup>11</sup>When goods increase, they increase who eat them, and what advantage has their owner but to see them with his eyes?<sup>12</sup>Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep.<sup>13</sup>There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches were kept by their owner to his hurt,<sup>14</sup>and those riches were lost in a bad venture. And he is father of a son, but he has nothing in his hand.<sup>15</sup>As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came, and shall take nothing for his toil that he may carry away in his hand.<sup>16</sup>This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain is there to him who toils for the wind?<sup>17</sup>Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger.<sup>18</sup>Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil with which one toils under the sun the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his lot.<sup>19</sup>Everyone also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil—this is the gift of God.<sup>20</sup>For he will not much remember the days of his life because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.
5.overview:
The Preacher turns to worship. Guard your steps when you go to the house of God; listening is better than the sacrifice of fools (v. 1). Because God is in heaven and you are on earth, words before him should be few (vv. 2-3). A vow to God must be paid, and it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (vv. 4-6). Many words are vanity, but God is the one you must fear (v. 7).

Oppression by officials should not surprise, for officials watch officials (vv. 8-9). He who loves money will not be satisfied with money; more goods bring more eaters, and the rich man cannot sleep (vv. 10-12). Hoarded riches are lost, and everyone leaves as naked as he came (vv. 13-17).

What is good and fitting is to eat, drink and enjoy one's toil in the days God gives. The power to enjoy wealth and accept one's lot is the gift of God, who keeps such a person occupied with joy (vv. 18-20).
5.theology:
Worship begins with listening and reverent fear, not many words (vv. 1-7; 1 Sam 15:22; Matt 6:7). God is in heaven, and in Christ believers may draw near with confidence and with reverence (Heb 4:16; 12:28-29). Promises to God are binding (vv. 4-6; Deut 23:21-23; Matt 5:37).

All earthly authority is accountable to a higher, and finally to God (vv. 8-9; Ps 82:1). The love of money cannot be satisfied and brings misery (vv. 10-17; 1 Tim 6:6-10); everyone leaves the world with nothing (v. 15; Job 1:21). Wealth, the power to enjoy it and contentment with one's lot are separate gifts of God (vv. 18-20; 1 Tim 6:17).
5.examples:
Coming to church to say your piece rather than to hear.

Promises made in hospital waiting rooms.

The lottery winner for whom enough keeps moving.

The labourer asleep and the rich man lying awake.

There are no pockets in a shroud.

A child too absorbed in play to watch the clock.

6.title: Wealth Without Enjoyment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Wealth Without the Power to Enjoy It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A grievous evil: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, and a stranger enjoys them (vv. 1-2). A man with a hundred children and many years, unsatisfied and unburied, is worse off than a stillborn child (vv. 3-5). Even two thousand years without good end in the one place (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Having everything is not the same as enjoying anything; enjoyment is a separate gift of God.

verseByVerse.quote: There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them. This is vanity; it is a grievous evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind:

Chapter 5 ended with the gift of joy. Chapter 6 shows its absence, and the Preacher says the evil lies heavy on mankind. This is not a rare case. It is common.

a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them. This is vanity; it is a grievous evil.

Here is the man who has everything. God has given him wealth, possessions, and honor. He lacks nothing. And God does not give him power to enjoy them. Put this beside 5:19, where the power to enjoy is the gift of God. Wealth and enjoyment are two different gifts. God can give the first and withhold the second.

That is one of the most searching truths in the book. Many people are praying for the first gift and never think to ask for the second. They imagine that if they only had the house, the job, the spouse, the money, they would be happy. But the capacity to be happy in them is not included in the purchase. It comes from God. And the man who has it all without that capacity watches a stranger enjoy what he worked for. Ask God for what you want if you must. Ask him first for a heart that can receive with joy what he has already given.

verseByVerse.quote: If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he. For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered. Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it finds rest rather than he.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he.

In Israel, many children and long life were the highest blessings a man could have. Here a man has both, in exaggerated measure: a hundred children, many years. But his soul is not satisfied, and at the end he is not even buried with honour. Scripture treats an unburied body as disgrace; Jeremiah said of a faithless king, With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried (Jer 22:19). The man with everything ends with nothing, not even mourners.

And the Preacher's verdict is shocking: a stillborn child is better off than he.

For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered. Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it finds rest rather than he.

The stillborn child never saw the light, never had a name spoken, never knew anything. Yet it finds rest. The rich man, who had everything, never did.

Parents who have lost a child before birth may find these verses hard to read, and they deserve a word. The Preacher is not saying the child's life did not matter. He is saying, from under the sun, that even the shortest life is not the worst fate. The worst fate is a long life with a restless soul. And the God who knows the name that was never spoken aloud has not lost that child.

verseByVerse.quote: Even though he should live a thousand years twice over, yet enjoy no good—do not all go to the one place?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even though he should live a thousand years twice over, yet enjoy no good—do not all go to the one place?

Double the longest life in Scripture, and more. Two thousand years. If a man enjoy no good, and the ESV notes that this may be rendered "see" no good, what has length added? Nothing, because all go to the one place (3:20).

Length of life is not the measure of it. A long life without joy is only a long walk to the same grave. A short life lived with God is full. Our culture spends fortunes trying to add years to life. The verse asks whether we have thought as hard about adding life to our years.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Who Knows What Is Good for Man?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied (v. 7). The wise and the poor have no final advantage (v. 8); what is in front of the eyes is better than wandering desire (v. 9). Man cannot dispute with one stronger than he, and more words only add vanity (vv. 10-11). For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The book's first half ends with a question only God can answer.

verseByVerse.quote: All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied. For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living? Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied.

We work to eat, and we eat, and we are hungry again. The ESV notes that satisfied is in Hebrew "filled". The appetite is like a vessel with a hole in the bottom. And it is not only the stomach. The deeper appetite of the soul is never filled by what we work for. Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? (Isa 55:2).

Jesus spoke to exactly this: Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you (John 6:27).

For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living?

The wise man's appetite is as unfilled as the fool's. The poor man who has learned good manners and good sense still goes hungry. Under the sun, wisdom and decency do not fill the hole.

Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind.

Here is practical wisdom, if not a final answer. Be content with what is in front of your eyes, rather than letting your desire wander after what you do not have. A bird in the hand. The meal on the table rather than the one in the advertisement. Yet even that contentment, on its own, is breath. It helps; it does not save.

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what man is, and that he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he. The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage to man?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what man is, and that he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he.

In Scripture, to name something is often to know it and to have authority over it. God determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names (Ps 147:4). Everything that exists has already been named, known and defined by God. And it is known what man is: a creature, made from the dust, and not God.

So man cannot argue with one stronger than he. He cannot take God to court and win. Isaiah said, Woe to him who strives with him who formed him (Isa 45:9), and Paul, But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? (Rom 9:20).

The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage to man?

Arguments with God multiply words, and words multiply breath. This echoes 5:2-3. When we cannot understand God, the answer is not more talk, but trust. Job came to the same place: after all his speeches, he laid his hand on his mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?

The first half of Ecclesiastes ends with two questions, and they are the right questions. What is good for us, in our short, breath-like life? The ESV's note marks vain as hebel again: a breath of a life. And what will happen after we are gone?

Life passes like a shadow. David prayed, Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding (1 Chr 29:15). Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow (Ps 144:4).

From under the sun, no one can answer these questions. That is the whole point. Chapters 7-12 will offer wisdom for how to live, but the final answer to "who knows what is good for man?" must come from above. And it has. He has told you, O man, what is good (Mic 6:8). And it has come in a person, who said, I came that they may have life and have it abundantly (John 10:10). The shadow is not the end for those who belong to him, because he is the light.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind:<sup>2</sup>a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them. This is vanity; it is a grievous evil.<sup>3</sup>If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he.<sup>4</sup>For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered.<sup>5</sup>Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it finds rest rather than he.<sup>6</sup>Even though he should live a thousand years twice over, yet enjoy no good—do not all go to the one place?<sup>7</sup>All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied.<sup>8</sup>For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living?<sup>9</sup>Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind.<sup>10</sup>Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what man is, and that he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he.<sup>11</sup>The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage to man?<sup>12</sup>For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?
6.overview:
The Preacher describes a heavy evil: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions and honour, but not the power to enjoy them, so that a stranger enjoys them instead (vv. 1-2). A man with a hundred children and many years whose soul is unsatisfied, and who is not even buried, is worse off than a stillborn child, who at least finds rest (vv. 3-5). Two thousand years without good still end in the one place (v. 6).

Man toils for his mouth and his appetite is never filled; the wise and the poor fare no better (vv. 7-8). What the eyes see is better than wandering desire (v. 9). Man cannot dispute with the one who is stronger, and more words only add vanity (vv. 10-11). The chapter ends with two questions: who knows what is good for man in his shadow-like life, and who can tell what will come after him? (v. 12).
6.theology:
Wealth and the power to enjoy it are separate gifts of God; he may give one and withhold the other (v. 2; 5:19). Neither long life nor many children can satisfy the soul (vv. 3-6). Human appetite is never filled by what it works for (v. 7; Isa 55:2), but Christ gives food that endures to eternal life (John 6:27).

God has named and defined all things, and man cannot contend with his Maker (v. 10; Isa 45:9; Rom 9:20). Life is a shadow (v. 12; Ps 144:4), and what is good for man is revealed by God, not discovered under the sun (Mic 6:8; John 10:10).
6.examples:
Praying for the house and never for a heart to enjoy it.

A hundred children and no mourners.

Adding years to life, and forgetting to add life to the years.

An appetite like a vessel with a hole in the bottom.

The meal on the table rather than the one in the advertisement.

7.title: Ecclesiastes 7 — Better-Than Proverbs: The Wisdom of Facing Reality

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Wisdom for the Realist: Better-Than Proverbs and the Search for Understanding
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 7 is the pivot of the book. The first half of Ecclesiastes (1–6) diagnosed the problem; chapters 7–12 begin developing the response. The chapter opens with a series of 'better than' proverbs that deliberately subvert conventional wisdom: the day of death is better than the day of birth; the house of mourning is better than the house of feasting; the rebuke of the wise is better than the song of fools. These are not counsel to morbidity but to realism—the person who can face death, sorrow, and correction has a firmer grip on reality than the person who seeks only comfort.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter's central section (vv. 13–22) counsels balance in the face of life's contradictions: prosperity and adversity both come from God; neither extreme righteousness nor extreme wickedness is prescribed; the fear of God navigates through both. Then vv. 23–29 record Qohelet's exhausting search for wisdom—finding it elusive—and his final conclusion: God made man upright, but humans have sought out many schemes. The chapter ends not with despair but with the diagnosis of the fall: the problem is not creation but corruption.
verseByVerse.examples: The 'better than' proverbs of vv. 1–14 are a masterclass in the theology of suffering and limitation. Keller: 'Ecclesiastes 7 is the wisdom book's equivalent of Romans 5:3—we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance. Qohelet's point is not that mourning is enjoyable but that it is honest and formative in a way that false mirth cannot be.' The house of mourning teaches what the house of feasting cannot: the truth about human finitude, and therefore the proper orientation toward God and neighbor.

verseByVerse.quote: A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of birth. It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A good name is better than precious ointment'—the Hebrew pun: shem (name) and shemen (ointment) sound alike. Character outlasts cosmetics. Then the provocative proverb: 'the day of death than the day of birth.' Not because death is pleasant but because death brings clarity: it reveals what a life was actually worth, what relationships were genuine, what investments lasted. 'The house of mourning'—at a funeral, human beings face the truth about themselves and each other with unusual honesty. The feasting house offers pleasure but not wisdom. The living 'lay it to heart': mortality is the great teacher of priorities.

verseByVerse.quote: Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad. The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By sadness of face the heart is made glad'—the paradox is exact: the external expression of grief produces an internal deepening of character that eventually issues in genuine gladness, not the surface gladness of the feasting house but the settled peace of a person who has faced reality. The wise person's heart is in the house of mourning—not morbidly, but because that is where truth is spoken and received. The fool's heart is in the house of mirth—not because mirth is bad but because the fool uses mirth as a substitute for reality rather than a fruit of it. Kidner: 'Joy built on avoidance is not joy but anesthesia.'

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools. For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of fools; this also is vanity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Rebuke of the wise'—painful to receive, productive in effect. 'Song of fools'—pleasant to hear, useless for formation. The image of thorns crackling under a pot is precise: thorns burn quickly and noisily, producing heat briefly and then ash. The laughter of fools is just such a blaze—impressive for a moment, useful for nothing. The wise person chooses the rebuke because they are oriented toward growth rather than comfort. Proverbs says the same: 'Better is open rebuke than hidden love' (27:5). Christian fellowship requires the courage to speak and the humility to receive correction.

verseByVerse.quote: Surely oppression drives the wise into madness, and a bribe corrupts the heart. Better is the end of a thing than its beginning, and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Oppression drives the wise into madness'—even wisdom is not immune to the distorting effects of sustained injustice. A bribe corrupts the heart of the just judge: no one is so wise that they are beyond corruption if the pressure is sustained. Then the proverbs of patience: the end of a thing is better than the beginning because the end reveals what the beginning promised. A building at completion is greater than a foundation. A life at its end is more fully known than at its beginning. 'Patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit'—patience is the fruit of trust in God's timing; pride insists on its own schedule.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart of fools. Say not, 'Why were the former days better than these?' for it is not from wisdom that you ask this. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Anger lodges in the heart of fools'—anger that dwells, that refuses to move on, that makes itself at home in the soul is the mark of foolishness. This is not a prohibition of righteous anger (Eph 4:26 permits anger without sin) but of the resentful, self-pitying anger that festers. 'Why were the former days better than these?'—nostalgia is not wisdom. The question assumes that the past was objectively better, which is rarely accurate and always unproductive. The wise person engages the present rather than mourning an idealized past. Kidner: 'Nostalgia is the mood of people who have given up on the present.'

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom is good with an inheritance, an advantage to those who see the sun. For the protection of wisdom is like the protection of money, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of him who has it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Wisdom and money are compared not to equate them but to show wisdom's superiority: money protects (through resources, influence, access), and wisdom also protects—but wisdom preserves life itself, not merely comfort.
